Merchant app · Order acceptance

Incoming
Orders

The five minutes a shop has to accept an order — and the promise it makes when it does.

05:00 to respond 23 screens 3 order channels 5 order states Mobile + desktop

Objective

Give a shop one screen that answers the only question that matters when an order lands: can we do this, and by when? The old accept flow treated every order the same — one button, no commitment, no sense of what the customer had been told. This redesign makes the shop's answer explicit, and makes it different depending on how the order is being fulfilled.

Three fulfilment channels and two timing modes produce six versions of the same screen. The goal was to handle all six without shipping six screens — one layout, driven by the order's own attributes, on both phone and desktop.

Why this screen carries the weight

  • A countdown is already running. The shop has 5 minutes to respond before the order times out, so nothing on the screen can require a second read. Most captures here show the clock already partway down.
  • Whatever the shop taps becomes a promise shown to the customer. An accept is not an acknowledgement — it sets the delivery or pickup estimate the customer then watches tick down.
  • The person tapping is mid-shift, one-handed, in a kitchen, or standing at a counter screen with a queue in front of them. The primary action has to be reachable without scrolling past the order contents.
  • A rejection costs the customer a meal and the shop a rating. Making the reason structured rather than free-text turns a bad moment into data operations can act on.

Context

BOX is a Greek food delivery platform. It runs two separate apps: one for customers and one for shops. This project sits entirely in the shop-side app — the navigation is Παραγγελίες, Κατάλογος, Κατάστημα, Ρυθμίσεις, and orders are the tab it opens on. It runs on a phone and as a desktop app on the counter.

The complication is that a shop does not always deliver its own food. Some orders it delivers with its own rider, some the customer collects, and some are picked up by BOX's own courier fleet. The shop's job — and therefore the wording of the button — changes in each case.

Five states

Every order sits in exactly one of five states, and the inbox is five counted tabs, one per state. The count is the label — a shop reads the number before it reads the word.

ΝέεςNew Σε εξέλιξηIn progress ΠρογραμματισμένεςScheduled ΟλοκληρωμένεςSuccessful ΑπορριφθείσεςRejected

The last two are terminal. Everything in this case study happens in the first three — and the whole design problem is the transition out of Νέες, which is the only one that runs on a timer.

Three channels, colour-coded

The order type is set once, at the top of the screen, in a single coloured word. That colour then carries through the scheduled-order banner, the list badges, the progress stepper and the time picker, so a shop can tell channels apart at a glance across the whole app.

Delivery

The shop's own rider

The shop prepares the order and delivers it itself. It owns the whole clock, door to door.

Commits to: delivery time
Take away

Customer collects

The customer walks in and picks it up. No rider, no address — the delivery block drops out of the screen entirely.

Commits to: ready time
Delivery από BOX

BOX's courier fleet

A BOX courier collects and delivers. The shop only controls preparation; the delivery estimate is not its to give.

Commits to: ready time

The channel labels shown here — Delivery, Take away, Delivery από BOX — are the current ones. The captures on this page predate that rename, so both delivery types still read Διανομή in the screens, separated only by colour. Naming them apart was the right call: to the customer both are simply a delivery, but to the shop they are two different jobs, which is why the button underneath them always differed.

Principles the screens had to hold

  • The accept action stays pinned to the bottom at every scroll position — a shop must never hunt for it while the clock runs.
  • The button says what it commits to, not what it does. No bare Αποδοχή.
  • A scheduled order announces itself before anything else, in a full-width tinted banner, because handling it now versus later is the first decision.
  • Changing the time is a peer of accepting, not buried in the accept flow — one tap away, on the same row.
  • Rejection is always available and always requires a reason.
  • Order contents come after customer and delivery details, since the shop reads who and where before what.
  • Every order carries a copyable reference so it can be quoted to support or the customer.
  • Customer notes — Σχόλια παραγγελίας — sit with the delivery details rather than with the items, because they are instructions for the handover, not the cooking. They appear on any channel, whenever the customer wrote something.

The flow

Five steps, in the order a shop meets them, with the phone and the desktop app shown together wherever the same state was captured on both. All screens are production Greek UI.

01

The inbox

The five state tabs, each carrying a live count. When a count is zero the tab is still shown — an empty inbox is information, not a blank screen. Desktop fits all five across the top at once; on the phone the strip scrolls, so four are visible and the fifth sits just off the edge.

02

A new order arrives

  1. Reference and rider slot, on one line. The order hash, the rider code (B620), and a copy button — everything needed to talk about this order to someone else.

  2. The countdown sits opposite the reference, in red, in a boxed monospace pair so the digits don't shift as they fall. It is the only red on the screen.

  3. Scheduled orders declare themselves in a tinted banner carrying the full date and a twenty-minute delivery window. Immediate orders get a plain timestamp instead — same slot, much quieter.

  4. Then the channel word, then customer details, then delivery details, then contents. Previous-order count sits in the customer block: a shop treats a ninth-time customer differently from a first.

  5. The action bar never scrolls away. On mobile, accept spans the full width and reject shrinks to an X on a second row; on desktop all three sit on one row.

03

Two ways out: change the time, or reject

Both secondary actions get their own surface, because both are decisions the shop should read properly — one sets a promise, the other cancels someone's dinner. On mobile they are full screens; on desktop they stack as a second modal, which keeps the countdown visible behind them. That is the better behaviour of the two.

04

Accepted — into the live list

Accepting moves the order from Νέες to Σε εξέλιξη and both counts update. Cards are dense on purpose: reference, rider code, timestamp, customer, address, item count, value, and channel — enough to identify an order without opening it.

05

The same screen, the other channels

Nothing structural changes. The channel word changes colour, the banner changes colour and verb — παράδοση becomes παραλαβή — the delivery-address block drops out for pickup, and the button commits to a different thing.

The commitment matrix

This table is the whole design decision in one place. Five combinations captured, five different promises, one layout. The wording is not cosmetic — each phrase names the clock the shop is actually accountable for.

Channel Timing Banner Primary action Change action
Delivery Immediate — Οκ, θα παραδοθεί σε 20′ Αλλαγή χρόνου παράδοσης
Delivery Scheduled Προγραμματισμένη παράδοση Οκ, ειδοποίησέ με 20′ πριν Αλλαγή χρόνου ειδοποίησης
Take away Immediate — Οκ, θα είναι έτοιμη σε 5′ Αλλαγή χρόνου προετοιμασίας
Take away Scheduled Προγραμματισμένη παραλαβή Οκ, ειδοποίησέ με 5′ πριν Αλλαγή χρόνου ειδοποίησης
Delivery από BOX Immediate — Οκ, θα είναι έτοιμη σε 15′ Αλλαγή χρόνου προετοιμασίας

Read down the primary-action column: delivered, notify me, ready, notify me, ready. Three verbs, and which one appears is decided by two attributes — who delivers, and when. A sixth combination exists too: a scheduled Delivery από BOX order, which carries a purple Προγραμματισμένη παραλαβή banner.

Why the rejection reasons are written out

A free-text rejection field produces unusable data and inconsistent customer messaging. Eight fixed reasons, each with an explanatory line, mean two different shops describe the same situation the same way — and each reason maps to a different message the customer should get.

Υψηλός Φόρτος Παραγγελιών

Too busy to prepare and deliver at quality and speed.

Capacity

Δεν υπάρχει διανομέας

No rider available to deliver the order.

Capacity

Μη Διαθέσιμο Προϊόν

At least one item is temporarily unavailable.

Catalogue

Εκτός ορίων εξυπηρέτησης

The address falls outside the delivery zone.

Coverage

Λάθος τιμή σε προϊόν

An item's price is out of date.

Catalogue

Κλείνουμε Σύντομα

Closing too soon to prepare the selected items.

Hours

Λόγω κακοκαιρίας

Weather prevents a rider reaching the area.

External

Άλλος λόγος

Free text — the only reason that needs typing.

Fallback

Four of the eight are things operations can fix — stock, price, zone, opening hours — which is the argument for structuring them at all.

After acceptance the clock flips

Before acceptance the countdown is a threat: respond or lose the order. After acceptance the same visual language becomes a progress ring on the list card, counting toward the promise the shop just made. Changes to that estimate arrive as inline cards inside the list rather than as toasts, so a shop that missed the notification still finds it.

The stepper, collapsed and open

An accepted order keeps the same layout but swaps the action bar for a stepper. Collapsed, it shows where the order is. Open, it shows when each stage happened — and on desktop the action becomes a single Ολοκλήρωση that moves the order into the successful state.

Biggest challenge

Three systems had to agree on one number. The customer app shows an estimate, the merchant app sets it, and for BOX-courier orders a separate fleet controls the half of the journey neither app owns. Getting one screen to state a commitment the other two would honour — and to update cleanly when the courier changed the pickup time — was harder than any individual layout.

The knock-on constraint was wording. Because the shop's accountability changes per channel, the button copy could not be a single string with a variable in it. Each combination needed its own sentence, reviewed in Greek, and each had to survive translation into the estimate the customer sees.

Expected impact

  • Fewer timed-out orders, because the decision and both escape hatches sit on one screen with the action bar always in reach.
  • More accurate customer estimates, because the shop states a time instead of accepting a default.
  • Rejection data operations can act on — unavailable items, stale prices and out-of-zone addresses become reportable rather than anecdotal.
  • Less inbound support contact, since scheduled orders resurface on their own and estimate changes persist in the list.

All screens are from the production Greek build of the merchant app, on Android and on the desktop app. Tap any screen on this page to see it full size.
